reason: The sources provide sufficient details to support a surprising 45-second story with well-supported claims.
story: Discovered in 1964 by a sounding rocket, Cygnus X-1 is the first black hole ever confirmed. Located roughly 7,000 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus, this stellar-mass beast is locked in a tight binary orbit with a blue supergiant star called HDE 226868. The pair circle each other every 5.6 days at a distance of just one-fifth the Earth-Sun distance. The black hole is constantly ripping away its companion's outer layers, forming a superheated accretion disk that glows brightly in X-rays. Recently, astronomers discovered that these twin jets of plasma are actually 'dancing'—wobbling back and forth due to the supergiant star's fierce stellar winds. These jets shine with the energy of 10,000 suns and blast outward at half the speed of light. In 1974, it was the subject of a famous bet between Stephen Hawking and Kip Thorne, where Hawking bet it wasn't a black hole as an insurance policy.
angle: The first confirmed black hole in history shoots twin plasma jets with the energy of 10,000 suns that visibly 'dance' and wobble at half the speed of light.

claims.claim: Cygnus X-1 was discovered in 1964 during a suborbital sounding rocket flight.
Cygnus X-1 is the first object widely accepted or confirmed to be a black hole.
It is located approximately 7,000 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus.
Cygnus X-1 forms a binary system with a blue supergiant star named HDE 226868.
The two objects complete an orbit around each other every 5.6 days.
The black hole and supergiant are separated by about 0.2 astronomical units.
The black hole continuously strips away material from the supergiant into an accretion disk.
The plasma jets from Cygnus X-1 travel at about half the speed of light.
The energy jets shine with the equivalent energy of roughly 10,000 suns.
The jets appear to bend or 'dance' because they are buffeted by strong stellar winds from HDE 226868.
Stephen Hawking and Kip Thorne made a famous friendly wager in 1974 over whether Cygnus X-1 was a black hole.
Stephen Hawking conceded the bet to Kip Thorne in 1990.

disputed: The exact mass of the black hole varies across studies, with older estimates and 2021 papers suggesting around 21 solar masses, while newer 2025 studies suggest a lower mass around 14 solar masses. Scripts should attribute these figures or describe the mass range.
